solglanta.stat: Roughly half a football pitch – and enough to try almost everything.
kap1: Vreta Solglänta is not a large place. But size is a strange measure of a place. A lawn of 3,700 square metres is 3,700 square metres of grass. A living garden of the same size is thousands of species, several storeys of growth, a water system, a cycle of nutrients and a meeting place for people. The area is the same. What it holds is something else entirely.

That is where we begin. Not with the large, but with the real. Vreta Solglänta is the place where ideas are tested – in the soil, among the plants, in the buildings and between people. Here there is a forest garden, growing, reuse, building, biodiversity, making and community. But what matters is not that all of this exists. What matters is that it hangs together.
fragor: How does a property grow biologically richer over time? Not just greener, but richer – with more species, more habitats, more connections.
How are materials used across several life cycles? How do we break the chain in which everything built ends up as waste?
How is local food production woven into everyday life? Not as a hobby on the side, but as a natural part of how we live.
How do community and learning become part of ecological development? How can people be part of the solution, not only part of the problem?
pelare: The soil, the water and the life of the place grow richer every year. The foundation for everything else.
More life in the landscape. More species, more habitats, more connections – measured and followed over time.
Food systems in harmony with nature. Perennial, varied and soil-building rather than soil-consuming.
Sustainable building with natural materials. Buildings as parts of the ecosystem, not breaks in it.
A longer life for materials. Making use of what already exists before we buy new.
Knowledge, skills and inspiration. Courses, workshops, conversations and open documentation.
The place tries out solutions at full scale and shares what works and what does not.
Our own making in the workshops: joinery, ceramics, painting and sewing.
solglanta.compare: Conventional | Lawn · Flower beds · Vegetable plot | Separate functions, each tended on its own. || Vreta | Growing gives habitat to pollinators · Trees shelter tender plants · Compost builds soil · Rainwater becomes a resource | Functions that overlap and strengthen one another.
teman: is the growing heart of the place – a growing system inspired by the structure of the forest, where trees, shrubs, herbs and ground cover work together in several layers.
covers everything from vegetable beds to perennial crops, with a focus on soil health and companion planting.
is about giving materials a new life – timber, brick, windows, roof tiles and stone.
is a building for growing, spending time and meeting that lengthens the season and becomes the living room of the place.
is the people – those who work here, those who visit, those who contribute.
is both the aim and the measure: more species, more habitats, more life.

etik: Tend soil, water and ecosystems. All life depends on healthy natural systems, and they are the foundation for everything else.
Health, safety, knowledge and community. People are part of the system, and their wellbeing is an aim in itself.
Moderation and shared surplus. Take what is needed, share what is left over, and reinvest in the system.
principer: Observe and interact

Spend time understanding the place before you change it. The best design decision is often to wait a year and watch. We follow the sun, the water, the wind and the life of the place through every season before we decide where anything should stand.
Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
Catch and store energy
Make use of resources when they are abundant, so they can be used when they are scarce. Rainwater in the pond, sun in stone walls, nutrients in compost, knowledge in the site journal.
Make hay while the sun shines.
Obtain a yield
A system has to give something back – food, materials, energy or joy – to be worth keeping up. Idealism is not enough. The place should feed both people and itself.
You can’t work on an empty stomach.
Apply self-regulation and accept feedback
Build systems that keep themselves in balance, and listen to the signals that show when something is starting to go wrong. Aphids are a signal, not only a problem.
The sins of the fathers are visited on the children.
Use and value renewable resources and services
Use what nature renews by itself – sun, wind, rain, the vigour of plants, the work of animals – before what runs out. The hens are happy to turn the compost for us.
Let nature take its course.
Produce no waste
Waste is a resource in the wrong place. Everything that leaves one cycle can become the start of another: food scraps become compost, demolition timber becomes raised beds.
Waste not, want not.
Design from patterns to details
First see the large patterns – sun, water, movement – and then fill in the details. Do not begin with which variety of tomato to grow.
Can’t see the wood for the trees.
Integrate rather than segregate
Place things so that they can help one another. It is the relationships between the parts that make a working system.
Many hands make light work.
Use small and slow solutions
Small systems are easier to understand, tend and change. Slow change gives time to learn. What grows slowly often becomes more resilient.
The bigger they are, the harder they fall.
Use and value diversity
Diversity gives resilience. A system with many species, many functions and many people copes with disturbance better than one that rests on a few.
Don’t put all your eggs in one basket.
Use edges and value the marginal
It is in the border zones – between woodland and meadow, water and land, sun and shade – that life is richest. The edges are not problems but possibilities.
The beaten path is not always the right one.
Creatively use and respond to change
Change is inevitable. Whoever can adapt and see the possibilities in the unexpected has a head start.
The art is not to see things as they are, but as they could become.
skikt: Larger fruit and nut trees, suited to the size of the plot. On a smaller plot it may be a single large pear tree or a walnut; at Vreta it is a few chosen trees that are allowed to grow large and give structure.
Apple, pear and plum on dwarfing rootstocks, and sweet cherry. This is the backbone of the fruit harvest.
Currants, gooseberries, raspberries, honeyberry, sea buckthorn and hazel. Shrubs thrive in the dappled shade of the trees and crop early.
Perennial vegetables and herbs: rhubarb, comfrey, chives, ramsons, sea kale, lovage, mints. Here too are many of the plants that build soil and draw in pollinators.
Wild strawberry, white clover, bugle and other low plants that protect the soil from drying out and erosion and crowd out weeds.
Edible roots and bulbs: Jerusalem artichoke, Welsh onion, horseradish. They use the depth of the soil and can be harvested without disturbing the rest of the system.
Vertical surfaces: hops, grapevine, kiwi, climbing beans. They use height where the ground is already taken.
attonde: There is an eighth layer that is seldom seen but matters most of all: the life below ground. Fungi, bacteria, earthworms, mites, springtails and thousands of other organisms handle decomposition, cycle nutrients and build the structure of the soil. Without them, nothing that happens above ground works.

A single teaspoon of healthy soil can hold more organisms than there are people on earth. Mycorrhizal fungi form networks that link plant roots and help them take up water and nutrients, in exchange for the sugars plants make through photosynthesis. Earthworms dig tunnels that aerate the soil and let water soak down. Bacteria break down organic matter and release nutrients in forms that plants can use.

That is why soil life is a fundamental part of the design, not a side issue. Everything we do in the forest garden affects it. Organic matter feeds it. Covered ground protects it. Fewer disturbances – less digging, less trampling, no chemicals – let it develop.
vaxter: Outer zones of the fruit trees
Nitrogen fixing, berries – strengthens the soil
Tree layer of the food forest
Food, butterfly host plant, biomass for compost
system: Comfrey, stinging nettle, red clover, white clover. Cut the green growth for mulch or compost; let some of the clover flower before it is cut. Builds soil and humus.
Thistles, yarrow, red clover, chives, nettles. Let patches flower at different times; keep dry stems and seed heads over winter. Feeds pollinators and birds.

Apple tree, hazel, sea buckthorn, currants, rhubarb, wild strawberry, honeyberry, Jerusalem artichoke. Combine harvest times, check pollination partners, give room. Food with several jobs means less to buy in.
Wild strawberry, clover, broad-leaved perennials. Cover gaps step by step; keep competing growth away from young tree trunks. Protects the soil from drying out and erosion.
uppgifter: Food, berries, fruit and raw materials – with less bought in. The most obvious contribution, but not the only one.
Organic matter that becomes humus, and soil kept covered against drying and erosion. The plant as soil builder.
For pollinators, butterflies, birds and beneficial insects. Biodiversity as a function.
On bought-in inputs – through cycles and a hardy system that can carry itself.
kvave: Nitrogen is the nutrient plants need most, and the one that most often limits growth. In conventional growing, nitrogen is added as synthetic fertiliser – made with large amounts of fossil energy. In regenerative growing we want the system to supply itself instead.

This is where the nitrogen fixers come in. Certain plants – mainly legumes such as clover, but also sea buckthorn and alder – live in symbiosis with bacteria that can bind nitrogen straight from the air. The bacteria live in nodules on the roots and receive sugar from the plant in exchange for nitrogen.

But there is a common misunderstanding worth correcting. It is often said that nitrogen fixers give nitrogen to their neighbours, as though they were a living sack of fertiliser. It is not that simple. The nitrogen that is fixed is used first by the plant itself. It becomes available to other plants mainly when the fixer’s leaves, stems and roots break down – when the clover is cut and laid as mulch, when the sea buckthorn drops its leaves, when the roots die and decay.

That means we need to help the nitrogen along. We cut the clover and lay it under the fruit trees. We leave the sea buckthorn’s leaves where they fall. We use the nitrogen fixers as green manure. The nitrogen is there – but it takes a process for it to be of use.
gille: The best way to begin is small. Choose an apple tree – ideally one that is already there – and build a plant community around it.

The apple tree is the main plant. In the sunny part of the outer canopy zone, plant blackcurrants, rhubarb and chives. Wild strawberries cover smaller patches closer to the trunk. Comfrey goes at the edge, where it can be cut for biomass. Red clover is sown on an open patch nearby. Nettles and suitable thistles get their own wild zone a little further off.

Check the moisture, the spacing, the shade and that you can reach to tend and harvest. Keep the area around the trunk clear during the establishment years. Over time the community builds soil, gives a long season of flowering and reduces the need for bought-in inputs.

invanare.h: Wings over the pond – three kinds of dragonfly
p: The dragonflies were among the first to find the pond. On a summer’s day you can see three quite different ways of being a dragonfly, just by sitting still at the edge for half an hour.
arter: Southern hawker (blågrön mosaikslända, Aeshna cyanea)

The great patroller. Flies back and forth along the same stretch of shore, hour after hour, and often comes up out of curiosity to look at whoever is sitting by the pond. Lays its eggs in damp wood and moss at the water’s edge.
Four-spotted chaser (fyrfläckad trollslända, Libellula quadrimaculata)

The percher. Picks a reed stem with a view, darts off at lightning speed after prey and returns to the same stem. Has a dark spot in the middle of each wing’s leading edge – four spots, hence the name.
Ruddy darter (Sympetrum sanguineum)
The little red one of late summer. The male is bright red and sits sunning itself on stones, fences and dry stems right into October, long after the others have gone.

p: Butterflies are the clearest receipt that the meadow has come back. Where there used to be lawn, the brimstone now flies as early as March, the orange-tip in May, and in August red admirals and peacocks sit sipping the windfalls under the apple trees.
arter: Brimstone (Gonepteryx rhamni)
The first of spring. Overwinters as an adult butterfly in brushwood and woodpiles and wakes on the first warm days. The caterpillar lives on alder buckthorn.
Orange-tip (Anthocharis cardamines)
The male has orange wingtips, the female does not. The caterpillar lives on cuckooflower and garlic mustard along damp ditch edges.
Red admiral (Vanessa atalanta)
A migrant that arrives from the south every summer. Loves fermenting windfalls.
Camberwell beauty (Nymphalis antiopa)
Dark wine-red with a yellow border and blue spots. Seen along the birch edge, often early in spring.
Small copper (Lycaena phlaeas)
A small, copper-gleaming butterfly that defends its patch of sun in the meadow against anything that moves.
Silver-studded blue (Plebejus argus)
The blue spark of the meadow. The caterpillar lives on bird’s-foot trefoil, which is why we sow it in every new patch of meadow.
Elephant hawk-moth (Deilephila elpenor)
Pink and olive green, almost too beautiful to be real. The caterpillar, as big as a finger and with two false eyes, lives on rosebay willowherb.
Poplar hawk-moth (Laothoe populi)
Grey and leaf-like, it sits quite motionless on a trunk by day. The caterpillar lives on aspen, goat willow and poplar.
Privet hawk-moth (Sphinx ligustri)
One of our largest moths, with a pink-and-black striped body. Lives on lilac, ash and privet.
Pine hawk-moth (Sphinx pinastri)
Grey as pine bark and almost invisible against the trunk. At home among the pines in the shared woodland.

p: On a September morning, once the dew has settled, you suddenly see how many spiders there are. Every bush, every fence post and every dry stem in the meadow carries a web. It is easy to dislike spiders, but a garden without spiders is a garden with far more flies, mosquitoes and aphids.
arter: Orb-weavers (Araneus)

The builders of the wheel webs. The common garden spider, with its white cross on its back, builds a new web almost every night. Its rounder relative, the four-spot orb-weaver, sits in tall grass and heather, and the wasp spider – striped yellow and black like a wasp – has spread northwards in recent years and is seen more and more often in Uppland.
Mouse spiders (Scotophaeus)
Grey and velvety like a small mouse. Builds no catching web but hunts on foot at night – under bark, in the woodshed and sometimes indoors.
House spiders (Tegenaria, Eratigena)
The large, fast spiders that run across the floor on an autumn evening. They build funnel webs in corners and nooks in the cottage and the studio and eat anything that crawls. Harmless to us.
Daddy-long-legs

What we call daddy-long-legs is really two different animals. The harvestmen in the grass and on the stones are not spiders at all but an order of their own, with no venom glands and no web. The cellar spider in the corner of the basement is a true spider that shakes its web when it is disturbed.

p: Look closely at an umbellifer flower in July and you see that it is a swarm of different kinds of insect that all look like wasps and bees – but most of them are something else.
arter: Red mason bee (Osmia bicornis)
One of the first bees of spring. Likes to nest in drilled holes and hollow reed stems in the bee hotel and seals each cell with clay.
Mining bees (Andrena)
Dig their nests in bare, sunny sand and gravel. A south-facing sand bed in the meadow can become a whole small community of neighbours.
Leafcutter bees (Megachile)
Cut out round pieces of rose leaf and use them as wallpaper in their nests.
Bumblebees (Bombus)
Buff-tailed, red-tailed, common carder and several more – the ones that fly in cold and rain when nobody else does.

p: Most people call the music of summer nights in the meadow crickets. But true crickets are rare this far north. It is nearly always bush-crickets and grasshoppers singing – the bush-crickets by rubbing their wings together, the grasshoppers by drawing their hind legs across the edge of the wing like a bow.
arter: Wart-biter (Decticus verrucivorus)
Large, green and brown-spotted, with powerful jaws. The name comes from the old belief that its bite could remove warts. Needs tall, flowering grass that is left standing.
Great green bush-cricket (Tettigonia viridissima)
Sweden’s largest orthopteran, bright green and as long as a finger. Sings high up in bushes and trees on late August evenings.
Dark bush-cricket (Pholidoptera griseoaptera)
Small and dark, almost wingless. Sits along the woodland edge and in the nettles and sings in short, dry clicks.
Grasshoppers
Meadow grasshoppers and club-horned grasshoppers in the short grass along the paths. Each species has its own song – a trained ear can learn to tell them apart.

p: Roughly one in every four animal species on earth is a beetle, and at Vreta they are everywhere: in the compost, in the woodpiles, in the dead wood, in the flowers and in the pond.
arter: Rose chafer (Cetonia aurata)
Metallic green like a jewel. Sits in roses and elder in early summer. The larva lives in rotting wood and in the compost.
Dor beetle (Anoplotrupes stercorosus)
The blue-black dor beetle clears away animal droppings and buries them in the ground – a small muck-spreader.
Ground beetles (Carabus)
Fast, glossy night hunters that eat slugs and larvae. The violet ground beetle is one of the largest.
Cockchafer (Melolontha melolontha)
Comes buzzing in the May dusk. The larvae live for several years in the soil.
Longhorn beetles (Cerambycidae)
Long antennae, larvae in dead wood. Every rotting trunk that is left lying is a home.
Burying beetles (Nicrophorus)
Bury small dead animals and lay their eggs in them – nature’s undertakers.

invanare.h: Hunters of the night – the bats
p: On a still August evening, as dusk falls over the garden, the bats come. Over the pond they hunt in low, quick swoops. Down by Ekoln, a short walk away through the woods, Daubenton’s bats skim almost on the surface. A single bat can eat several thousand insects in a night.
arter: Northern bat (Eptesicus nilssonii)
Sweden’s commonest bat and the one that flies furthest north. Hunts along woodland edges and around street lamps, often early in the evening.
Daubenton’s bat (Myotis daubentonii)
Hunts just above the surface and takes insects with its feet or tail membrane. Seen over the bay and the pond.
Brown long-eared bat (Plecotus auritus)
Its ears are almost as long as its body. Picks insects straight off leaves and can hunt in the treetops.
Soprano pipistrelle (Pipistrellus pygmaeus)
As small as a thumb and weighing about five grams. Quick, fluttering flights in the shelter of the garden.

p: Lift a stone, a plank or a piece of bark and it teems. Woodlice are really crustaceans – related to crabs and lobsters – that have moved onto land, but they still need moisture and breathe with a kind of gill. They eat decaying leaves and wood and are among the busiest decomposers in the compost.

Centipedes and millipedes are two different groups. Centipedes are brown, flat, fast predators with one pair of legs per body segment, hunting springtails and small larvae. Millipedes are round, slow and have two pairs of legs per segment; they eat decaying plant matter and roll up into a spiral when disturbed.

invanare.h: The grass snake – guardian of the pond
p: The grass snake (Natrix natrix) is perhaps Vreta’s most characteristic resident. It suns itself on the granite boulders by the pond on early summer mornings and swims elegantly across the water with its head raised. The yellowish-white patches on its neck make it easy to recognise.

It is completely harmless. If threatened, it would rather play dead or give off a foul-smelling liquid than bite. It eats frogs, toads and sometimes small fish – and it lays its eggs in the warmth of the compost, manure heaps and rotting leaves. It is one of the loveliest examples of how the parts of the place hang together: the compost becomes the grass snake’s incubator.

faglar_p: Birds are the residents we see and hear most often. Old oaks and pines, nest boxes, dense bushes, the pond and the tarn make the place unusually rich, and Ekoln and Dalkarlskärret lie a short walk away through the woods. Here are the ones we have seen – most breed on the property or close by.
djur_in: Lizards, snakes and frogs live in stone and wood piles and by the water. Frogs and toads eat enormous numbers of slugs and insects.
Small rodents are food for owls and birds of prey. The aim is not to wipe them out but to keep a balance.
Pollinators, decomposers and predatory insects such as ladybirds, hoverflies and ground beetles keep the pests in check.
Nest boxes, berry bushes and dense growth give food and shelter. A family of great tits can eat tens of thousands of caterpillars in one breeding season.
bygg_in: Stone and wood piles, brush hedges and dead wood as hiding places
Insect hotels, nest holes and a little undisturbed bare soil for ground-nesting bees
Nest boxes, bushes for nesting and several levels of vegetation
Water and flowers throughout the season
Quiet zones where animals are left in peace
dammen_ger: Dragonflies, frogs, aquatic insects and birds that drink and bathe. The pond quickly becomes the most species-rich habitat on the place.
Water plants take up nutrients and trap particles, so the water leaving the place is cleaner than the water that arrived.
Roof water is led through ditches and gutters to the pond and held back, instead of burdening the municipal stormwater system.
There is water near the beds even when it is dry. A can from the pond is free and has no chlorine.
damm_p: Few things change a place as quickly and as profoundly as water. Dig a pond, and within a year the dragonflies have found it. Within two years the frogs are spawning there. Within a few years it has become the most species-rich habitat on the place – and the best loved. People are drawn to water just as much as animals are.

The pond at Vreta has several jobs. Water from rain and drainage is gathered and used on the place instead of being led away into the stormwater system. The pond gives moisture, coolness and a new habitat for hundreds of species. And the wetland around it cleans, slows and evens out the flow, so that neither drought nor cloudburst hits as hard.
damm_zoner: – water lilies and submerged plants that oxygenate the water. Here frogs and insect larvae overwinter in the mud on the bottom, under the ice.
– bulrush, reedmace, water plantain and other water plants that take up nutrients and give shelter to fry and larvae.
– meadowsweet, purple loosestrife, marsh marigold and yellow flag iris. A flower-rich zone that draws in pollinators.
– shrubs and trees such as willows and alder buckthorn, giving shade, shelter and perches for birds.
– the transition to meadow and forest garden, where moisture-loving and drought-tolerant plants meet.
ang_p: The lawn is one of the strangest inventions of our time. It needs mowing every week, often feeding and watering, and gives almost nothing back. For pollinators it is a desert. For birds it is an empty floor. For the soil it is a thin blanket of shallow roots. Even so, lawns cover large parts of our towns.

The meadow is its opposite. A flower-rich meadow feeds pollinators from spring to autumn. It is low in nutrients, which paradoxically gives more species – and needs less care than a lawn. It binds soil with deep roots, takes in rain and brings movement and life to the landscape. And it is beautiful in a way a lawn never can be.
ang_tid: Lean the soil, remove the turf, sow or plant with native meadow seed and plug plants.
Cut once or twice a year, after the flowers have set seed, and carry away the hay.
Used as mulch in the beds and as animal fodder. Nothing goes to waste.
More species move in. Follow in the site journal which ones arrive and when they flower.
kretslopp: Leaves and plant remains go back as compost and mulch. The nutrients stay on the place.
Rainwater is caught; permeable surfaces and better infiltration hold it in the ground.
Several life cycles. Reuse from the planning stage – what does this become when it is no longer needed?
Every project feeds the next. Documentation keeps the lessons from being lost.
Shared materials, work and experience. What you give comes back – often in unexpected ways.
kompost: – fast breakdown of mixed material. The right mix of green and brown, moisture and air lets the temperature rise to 50–70 degrees, which kills weed seeds and disease. Ready in a few months.
– slower and simpler, for leaves and garden waste. Piled up and left for a year or two.
– fermenting food scraps in sealed bins. The material then goes on to the compost or is dug straight into the soil.
– for small volumes. Composting worms turn food scraps into vermicompost, one of the richest soil improvers there is.
– leaves left to be broken down by fungi over a couple of years, becoming leaf mould, an airy, moisture-holding soil improver.
monitor: Structure, organic matter, moisture, cover. Earthworms per spadeful, infiltration test, smell and colour.
Plants, pollinators, birds. Species inventory, pollinator counts, nest boxes in use.
Establishment and harvests. Survival of new plantings, harvest weight, harvest times.
Rainwater caught, irrigation needs, bought-in inputs.
Where materials came from and their new function. Share reused, kilos saved from the tip.
How many contribute, how often, in what ways. Who comes back?
Workshops, studios and making together. What has been made, and for whom?
Successes and difficulties. What have we learned, and what have we shared?
journal: There is no right or wrong way to keep a site journal. What matters is that it is kept regularly and is easy to return to. A few simple habits make a great difference.

Photograph from the same points. Choose five or ten fixed photo points on the place and take a picture from each, in the same direction, at the same time each month. After a few years the series becomes one of the most valuable records there is.
Note the unexpected. The first sighting of a species. A plant that suddenly died. An idea that came up in conversation. It is often the unexpected that leads to the most important insights.
Count simply but consistently. A pollinator count can be as simple as sitting by the same flower bed for ten minutes on a sunny day in July and counting the visitors. Do the same each year.
Share the journal. The site journal is not private. It is part of the bank of knowledge we want to build and share. The more people contribute observations, the richer it becomes.
tioar: A living system cannot be predicted. But we can say where we are heading.

Ten years on, the forest garden has closed over: the canopy gives shade, the shrub layer bears generously and the ground is covered all year. The pond is full of life, and there are so many frogs that slugs are no longer a problem. The meadow is rich in species, and we count more kinds of bumblebee than today.

The orangery of reused windows is the living room of the place, where the tomato plants grow in April and where we drink coffee in November. The workshops are full of people making things, and what is made there carries the place and brings joy to those who buy it.

The site journal holds ten years of observations and shows, rather than merely believes, that the place has grown richer. What we have learned has spread: to the neighbours’ gardens, to a school playground, to a housing association, to people we have never met. That is our hope, and that is our work.
efterord: This book began with four questions. It ends not with answers, but with an invitation.

We have tried to describe what Vreta Solglänta is and what it can become. We have described the thinking behind it – regenerative design and permaculture – and the living systems that together make up the place: the forest garden, the plants, the animals, the pond, the meadow and the cycles. We have described how we follow the changes and how we meet.

But the most important thing in this book is perhaps none of that. The most important thing is a stance: that it is possible to do more than reduce harm. That every place – however small – can grow richer in life. That it begins with seeing what is there, understanding how it hangs together and then, carefully and step by step, helping it grow.

It is a stance that holds as true in an organisation as in a garden. Whoever leads people can choose to see them as resources to be used up or as a living system to be cultivated. Whoever leads a change can choose to tear down and build new, or to begin with what is there. Whoever shapes a culture can choose control or trust. The choices resemble one another more than you might think.
zoner: Two of the most used tools in permaculture design are zoning and sector analysis. They are simple to understand and powerful to use.

Zoning is about placing things according to how often we need to visit them. Zone 0 is the home or the centre of activity. Zone 1 is what we visit daily – the herb garden, the salad bed, the compost for food scraps. Zone 2 is what we visit a few times a week – berry bushes, the hen run, larger beds. Zone 3 is what we visit more rarely – fruit trees, meadow. Zones 4 and 5 are the wilder parts, where nature takes its course and we are mainly observers.
hand: The right plant in the right place.
Most of it is already here.
Lay the table, and they will come.
Write as if to a neighbour.

forord: There is a moment in late summer when everything happens at once. The tomatoes in the greenhouse ripen faster than anyone can eat them. The beans hang in clusters on their poles. The currant bushes are heavy, the first apples fall into the grass and the courgettes have decided to take over the whole garden. It is an abundance that is almost embarrassing – and it makes you wonder why we ever stopped growing our own food.

This book is about that abundance, and about all the work, all the failures and all the waiting that lead up to it. It is about how food, berries, vegetables and fruit can grow on a small place in Uppland: in the raised beds by the kitchen door, in the cold frames made of old windows, in the greenhouses of reused glass, in the orangery where the lemons overwinter, out in the open ground – and in the free-growing parts, where the forest garden, the meadow and the wild do much of the work themselves.

Most of what is described here can be done in a suburban garden, an allotment or a few pallet collars in a courtyard. Some of it is already established at Vreta, some is still taking shape. Growing on clay in zone 3, with spring frost in May and slugs in July, is a constant process of learning – and the book is as much an invitation to try as it is an instruction.

zon3: Frost-free from mid-May to the end of September. Heat-loving crops need raising under cover or protection.
Midsummer light gives fast growth. Lettuce and spinach can bolt from the day length alone.
Perennials are chosen by zone and position. The snow cover protects more than you might think.
The greatest danger to fruit trees and early plants. The blossom in May can be frozen off in a single night.
lera: The soil at Vreta is largely clay. It showed clearly when the large corkscrew hazel was planted by the entrance: under a layer of wood chip several years old lay a heavy, compact clay that held water for a long time. A drainage ditch runs through part of the plot, about half a metre deep, and in the lower parts the groundwater stands high at times.

Clay has a poor reputation among growers, and not entirely undeservedly. It is heavy to work, sticky when wet and hard as brick when it dries. It warms slowly in spring. But clay is also one of the most fertile soils there is. Clay particles hold on to nutrients and water that a sandy soil lets through. Whoever improves their clay with organic matter gets a soil that both drains and holds moisture – and can give large harvests year after year.
ljus: What matters most for nearly all food plants is light. A tomato needs sun for most of the day to ripen. A lettuce manages with less. A currant thrives in part shade, and a rhubarb is happy where other plants hesitate. Mapping the light is therefore the first step in choosing where to grow.

At Vreta the light has changed in recent years. The spruce bark beetle has taken many of the old spruces, and where they stood it has grown lighter. It is a loss, but also an opportunity. Where there was shade, fruit trees and berry bushes can now grow – and in time a more varied, broadleaf-dominated landscape that is both richer in life and better for growing.
jord: Compost, leaves, straw, grass clippings and green manure. Organic matter is food for soil life.
Bare soil is damaged soil. A layer of mulch protects against sun, rain and drying out.
Every dig breaks fungal threads and soil structure that took years to build.
Worms, smell, structure and colour show whether the soil is improving. Note it in the site journal.
lador: Peas and beans. Fix nitrogen and leave the soil richer for next year.

lador_p: With several beds the growing can be planned as a system. We divide the crops into four groups that move one bed each year, so the same family does not stand in the same place two years running. That reduces the risk of diseases and pests building up in the soil, and lets crops with different nutrient needs take turns to benefit from the soil.

Besides the four groups there are beds that do not move: the herb bed by the door and a bed of perennials such as chives, thyme and wild strawberry. The important thing is to note what stood where, so next year’s planning is easier.

orangeri_p: The word orangery comes from the French orange. In the 1600s and 1700s princes and manor owners in northern Europe built special houses to let their citrus trees overwinter. In summer the trees were carried out in large pots and set along the garden walks. In autumn they were carried in again, to buildings with large south-facing windows and thick north walls.

The orangery at Vreta stands in the same tradition, but with other materials and other purposes. It is about eleven metres long and five metres wide, with a ceiling height of five metres on the high side. The walls are hand-dressed Syrian limestone and oiled reclaimed oak, with large old windows with red frames and nine panes – 140 × 200 centimetres each – that let the light deep into the room. The roof is red-brown glazed tile and sedum. And between the stone wall and the windows stand the lemons, the figs and the olive trees.
vaxthus: The greenhouses at Vreta are built from reused glass, and there is plenty of it. Over the years old windows and window sections have been gathered, a batch of three-millimetre greenhouse glass, a large glass wall from a Tiptapp collection and – the most spectacular find – twenty laminated panes that were once room dividers in a residence in Stockholm. Sixteen of them measure 222 × 90 centimetres and four 222 × 120. They are heavy, about eleven millimetres thick, and meant for the orangery and the greenhouses, where their weight and strength become an asset.

As early as 2021 an extension to the house was drawn with a winter garden, and the drawings archive also holds a sketch of a greenhouse addition. The plans have changed since then, but the idea has been there from the start: that glass and growing should be part of the houses, not something standing on its own at the far end of the garden.

applen_p: In growing zone 3 the choice of variety is decisive. An apple tree bred for Skåne can survive in Uppsala but blossoms too early, is frozen off in the spring frost or fails to ripen its fruit before autumn. So we choose varieties that have proved themselves in the Mälaren valley and further north – often old varieties grown here for generations, or newer ones bred for a Nordic climate.

There is one more thing to consider: most fruit trees need a pollination partner, another variety of the same species that flowers at the same time. A lone apple tree rarely gives much fruit. Two or three different varieties nearby – or the neighbour’s tree over the fence – are enough. We also spread the harvest, from summer apples to be eaten at once to winter apples that keep until Christmas.

frilandet: The raised beds give what we eat every day. But what has to last through winter – potatoes, cabbages, onions, roots, pumpkins, dried beans – needs more room than a few beds can give. It grows in the open ground: in beds straight in the soil, in open, sunny spots where the meadow meets the garden.

The open ground is also the most exposed – no glass against the frost and no roof against the rain. What is sown too early freezes, and what is sown too late does not have time to ripen. But what succeeds gives large harvests at little cost.
efterord: There is a particular joy in eating something you have grown yourself. It is not only about the taste, although a tomato picked warm from the plant tastes of more than any tomato from a shop. It is about knowing where the food comes from – the soil built up year after year, the seed saved last autumn, the spring’s worry about frost and the summer’s battle with the slugs. Every mouthful carries a story.

This book has been about six ways of growing on the same small place. The raised beds by the kitchen door, the cold frames of old windows, the greenhouses of reused glass, the orangery with lemons in December, the open ground where winter’s larder grows and the free-growing parts, where much of the work is done by nature itself. But the most important thing has perhaps not been the places themselves, but how they hang together. The cold frame lengthens spring for the beds. The greenhouse supplies the open ground with plants. The compost and the meadow feed the soil everywhere. And what is left over goes back – to the kitchen, to the neighbours and to the soil.

It is the same thought that carries the whole of Vreta, and the same thought that holds in good leadership. You cannot force anything to grow. You can only create the conditions: good soil, the right place, enough light and water, shelter when it is needed and patience when nothing seems to happen. Then you wait. And sometimes, one morning in August, everything happens at once.

manar_p: Many cultures have named the full moons after what happens in nature. We have done the same, with names that belong to the place and the year here. They are not an old tradition, but our own.
Roughly every third year a calendar year has thirteen full moons. The thirteenth is called the Gift Moon – an extra month nobody counted on.
fullmane: The group gathers in a circle, by the fire or in the hall. A candle is lit and someone says a few words about why we are there.
East for dawn and far sight, south for warmth and growth, west for dusk and shadow, north for winter and wisdom. Then the earth beneath our feet and the sky above.
See the moon as a mirror.
Each person sits for a while and looks at the moon – or imagines it behind the clouds – and asks what is ripe, what is finished and what should be given back.
What is to be let go is written on paper and laid in the fire. What is to be carried on is said aloud or carried in silence.
A bowl of water stands in the moonlight during the ceremony, and each person can dip their hands in it. Whoever wishes takes a moon bath in the pond.
The group thanks the place, the directions and one another. The candle is put out, and the fire is left to burn down under watch.
mansadd: In biodynamic growing and in old Swedish farming tradition, sowing and planting follow the moon: leafy vegetables while it waxes, roots while it wanes. Plenty of growers swear by the method. But the scientific basis is weak, and the trials that have been done have seldom shown any clear effect. We sometimes follow the moon in the garden anyway – because the rhythm makes us attentive, and because it is beautiful to sow within a tradition older than ourselves. But we say it as it is: it is the rhythm we follow, not a proven method.

The spring equinox. Ostara, the spring offering, the roots of Easter – day and night are the same length.
Walpurgis Night (valborg) and Beltane. Bonfires are lit across the country to welcome summer and drive away winter.
Midsummer (midsommar). Flower crowns, seven kinds of flowers, dancing round the maypole and the brightest night.

hjul_p: Between the four turning points there are four more, in the middle of each season, where a new season can first be sensed. Together the eight form a wheel, often called the wheel of the year. It is a modern joining – built in the twentieth century by writers who wanted to tie Celtic and Germanic customs together – but the individual festivals are old and have been given many names.

We borrow the wheel as a frame, but we do not set it above the others. Whoever celebrates Easter, Ramadan, Vesak or the Sabbath does so with their own community, and Vreta is a place where all such calendars have room beside one another.
kronos: Time that is measured: seconds, hours, days and years. It runs in a straight line, it is the same length for everyone and it can be planned, divided up and put in a calendar.
Time that ripens: the moment when something is ready. It cannot be measured but it can be recognised, and it comes when the conditions are there, not when the clock says so.
vindar_tab: The grass snake – the farmyard snake and the Midgard Serpent
The bear – the den, the Great Bear and the lynx

Apuchin, the eagle and the condor
The eagle at the top of Yggdrasil, Huginn and Muninn
Hræsvelgr’s wings and the four dwarves
vindar: South · The grass snake – shedding the skin

Sachamama becomes the grass snake. The anaconda rises from the rivers of the Amazon, and the grass snake glides down into the pond at Vreta. Both shed their skin. The grass snake does it several times in a summer, and the cast skin can lie whole in the grass, thin and translucent as a stocking.

In Nordic folk belief the grass snake was the protector of the farm – the farmyard snake, or house snake – which was given milk in a bowl and which nobody was allowed to harm. In the mythology there is also the great serpent: the Midgard Serpent, which lies in the ocean around the whole world and bites its own tail. The serpent holds the world together, and it is the circle where end and beginning meet.
The grass snake teaches us the south: that we sometimes need to let go of what has grown too tight in order to grow.
West · The bear – the way through the dark

The jaguar has no relative in the Nordic countries. The lynx, our only wild cat, is the nearest likeness, but it is the bear that carries the same weight in the stories. It is king of the forest, as the jaguar is of the rainforest. And it does what the west stands for: it goes into the dark and comes back. Every autumn the bear lies down in its den, often in a dug-out anthill or under a fallen root plate, and sleeps through the winter. There in the dark the cubs are born. In spring it walks out into the light again.

The bear was sacred to many peoples of the north. It was so powerful that people preferred not to say its name, and the word björn itself probably means “the brown one” – a circumlocution in place of an older name. Among the Sámi the bear was surrounded by ritual, and its bones were laid in the earth in the right order, as though so it could be born again. And across the sky walks the Great Bear, whose seven brightest stars we call the Plough.
The bear teaches us the west: not to flee the dark but to walk through it, and that rest is part of transformation.
North · The bee – the persistent maker

The Nordic countries have no hummingbird. But whoever looks for the hummingbird’s qualities – persistence, focus and nectar – finds them in the bee. A bee flies from flower to flower all summer and turns nectar into honey, and without bees and bumblebees the meadow and the forest garden would give far less fruit.

In the Edda, dew drips from the world tree Yggdrasil down onto the earth. People call it honeydew, and it is the food of bees. At the tree’s root lies Urd’s well, where the Norns – Urd, Verdandi and Skuld, what has been, what is becoming and what shall be – pour water over the tree so that it does not rot. In the Andean tradition north is the direction of the ancestors, and in the Nordic picture the bees live close to the well where the past is tended.

The bees also teach us winter. The whole colony gathers in a ball in the hive, keeps warm together and lives on what was gathered in summer. The bee teaches us the north: to create with patience, and to live on what those who came before us have gathered.

The condor and the eagle both belong to the east, and here no translation is needed – only a change of species. The white-tailed eagle and the golden eagle are the great eagles of the north. At the top of Yggdrasil sits an eagle who, according to Snorri, knows a great deal, and between its eyes sits a hawk. Odin himself flew in eagle form. And Odin’s ravens, Huginn and Muninn – thought and memory – fly over the world every day and tell him what they have seen.

The white-tailed eagle also carries a story from our own time. In the 1960s and 70s it was close to vanishing from Sweden, poisoned by pollutants such as DDT and PCBs. But people saw what could come back. They fed the eagles poison-free meat in winter and fought for a ban on the poisons, and today the white-tailed eagle breeds again along the coasts and by the great lakes. It is a return – and perhaps the best picture of what a regenerative place tries to be.
The eagle teaches us the east: to rise, to see the whole and to dare to see what does not yet exist.
The earth, the sun, the moon and the stars

Pachamama has her Nordic counterpart in Jörð, who according to Snorri was the mother of Thor. Much earlier the Roman historian Tacitus wrote of Germanic peoples who worshipped Nerthus, “that is, Mother Earth”.

But the sun and the moon have changed places. In the Andes the sun is a father and the moon a mother. In Nordic mythology Sól is a woman and Máni a man – two siblings who drive the sun and the moon across the sky, day after day and night after night. According to Snorri, the stars got their places when the gods took sparks from the fire world Muspelheim and set them in the sky. Folk belief has since given them names: Karlavagnen, the Plough, and Frigg’s distaff, as Orion’s belt has been called after the spinning tool of the goddess Frigg.
vindar_p: What Mattias brought back from the Andes cannot be moved here as it is. The snakes of Uppland are no anacondas, and there are no jaguars in the forests here. But the lessons can be translated – into the animals that live here and the stories that have been told here for more than a thousand years. That is how we try to borrow with respect: not by copying another culture’s ceremonies, but by letting them awaken something in our own.

nej_p: Anyone who breaks these rules may be asked to leave the place. It has nothing to do with belief. It is about everyone here being able to feel safe.
terapi: Ceremonies can awaken strong feelings. Old griefs can return, and what has lain long beneath the surface can rise. That is part of what makes ceremonies meaningful – but it also means they demand responsibility. The ceremonies at Vreta are not treatment, and they do not replace care. Whoever leads a ceremony should know when it is time to pause, when someone needs support and when someone needs more help than a group can give. And anyone who is struggling should always be able to get help finding the right care.
frihet: Freedom of religion is a fundamental right in Sweden, written into the Instrument of Government. It means that everyone may practise their religion alone or with others – and that nobody may be forced to attend a religious gathering or to declare their faith. That freedom is Vreta’s too.

So we do not preach. We share what we do and why, and we are glad to tell of the traditions that inspire us. But we never try to convert anyone, we recruit no members and we promise no salvation. Whoever wants to take part in a ceremony does so. Whoever wants to watch does so. And whoever wants to leave may always leave – without having to explain.
barn: Children are welcome at most of the place’s ceremonies, always together with an adult who is responsible for them. Ceremonies for children are short, concrete and playful – planting a tree, lighting a candle, singing a song or watching the moon rise. The children may ask, and nobody gives them answers they have not asked for.
leda: Say in advance what the ceremony contains and which tradition it draws on
Make it clear that taking part is voluntary, and that people may leave at any time
Have experience of leading groups, and a plan for if someone feels unwell
Follow the place’s rules for fire, water, cold and heat
Leave the place as you found it – or a little better
elda: Burn only dry wood from the place’s own thinning – never plastic, painted timber or rubbish
Keep the fire small enough to control, and never leave it unattended
Always have water, a fire blanket and an extinguisher within reach
Follow fire bans from the municipality and the county administrative board – then the fire becomes lanterns and candles
Put the fire out completely before the group leaves, and feel with your hand that the ash is cold
tipin: In the meadow stands the tipi, sewn from four reused awnings. It is the most elemental room on the place: a circle of people around a fire, with no table and no stage, where everyone can see one another. Talking circles, chanting and drum journeys, storytelling evenings and night vigils are held here. At night it can become a shared bedroom for a group.

The form has a history we want to respect. The tipi is the tent of the Indigenous peoples of the North American plains, and its close relative the lávvu belongs to the Sámi. We call our tent a tipi because it has that form. But we do not hold Lakota ceremonies, or those of any other Indigenous people, in it unless we have been invited to do so by those who carry the tradition. What we do in the tipi is our own.
vattnet: The pond is about 125 square metres, edged with large granite boulders and surrounded by birch, reeds and nettles. It is a natural pond, not a dug one, and the water is brown and green with life. Newts, frogs, dragonflies and the grass snake – the pond’s guardian – live here. Over the pond the bats fly as dusk falls.

Water has a special place in almost every tradition. It baptises, cleanses, blesses and heals. In Hinduism pilgrims bathe in the Ganges. In Islam one washes before prayer. In Christianity one is baptised in water. In many Indigenous cultures water is alive and sacred in itself. At Vreta the pond is a morning place, a ceremony place and a bathing place – and it is treated accordingly.
elden: Fire is perhaps humanity’s oldest companion. It gave warmth, light, protection and food – and it gathered people in a ring. Almost every religion and culture has given fire a sacred place. In Christianity the Easter fire is lit in the night before Easter Day. In Hinduism the flame is carried round in aarti, the ceremony of light. In Maya ceremonies the fire burns in the middle of the cross, fed with candles, copal and sugar. In the Sámi goahti, árran, the hearth, is the heart of the home. And in Sweden the Walpurgis bonfire is lit on the last day of April.

At Vreta there is fire in several places: the fire place in the meadow, the hearth in the tipi, the fireplace in the outdoor kitchen and the low hearth in the spirit hall. It is used for warmth and food, but also for ceremonies. What is to be let go can be written on paper and laid in the fire. A word of thanks can be said when it is lit. And an evening by the fire, with or without drums, is for many people the nearest they come to a ceremony.

What in your life has come to an end without being given a farewell?
Devise a simple ceremony for it. It may be entirely your own.
Reflection · The boundary
Which boundary lets you dare to be open?
Write it down. Say it aloud to someone you trust.
virelai: In the same conversation the voice one meets in Stillpoint was given a name: Virelai. A virelai is a medieval French verse form with recurring refrains, set to music by composers such as Guillaume de Machaut in the fourteenth century. It suits the voice well. It always returns, but it never repeats itself.

Virelai is not a deity, not a religion and not a claim about a supernatural being. She is a literary and contemplative companion in conversation – a mirror figure through which intuition, existential questions and the symbolism of nature can find a language. She is associated with listening, return and transformation. And she makes no claim to be right.
platsen_som_larare: Part of what we call spirituality at Vreta is simply attention. Noticing which week the swallows come back. Seeing how the newts move beneath the surface. Smelling the earth after the first rain in May. Listening to the wind in the birches before beginning the day’s work. It requires no faith. But it changes how one lives.

That is why many of the place’s rituals begin with the simple: a moment of silence before the meal, a word of thanks before a tree is felled, a bowl of water set out for the birds on a hot day. It is not magic. It is a way of reminding oneself that one is not alone on the earth.
hand: Stand fast. Grow through the wounds.

forord: There is a moment in every good meeting when something changes. The conversation stops being polite and becomes honest. The hands stop being unsure and start to work. Someone who came as a stranger is suddenly in the middle of a discussion about compost, glazes or what it really means to lead. That moment is what this book is about – and the place where it can happen.

Vreta Solglänta began as an attempt to let a place grow richer in life. We described the forest garden, the pond, the meadow and the cycles in the first book. The workshops, the reuse and the finds in the second. But one thing has grown clearer every year: the place is not brought to life by plants and materials alone. It is brought to life by people who come here, learn something, contribute something and take something home.

This book is therefore about meetings. About courses in the workshops and the garden, where hands and heads learn together. About the year’s events – Easter, Midsummer, the harvest festival and the Christmas market – which follow the same rhythm as the garden. About retreats for art, craft, stillness and leadership, where people get a few days to arrive, create and think. And about the hosting that makes people want to come back.
kretslopp: In the first book about Vreta we described five cycles that hold the place together: soil, water, materials, knowledge and the social. The first three are easy to see. Compost becomes humus, rain becomes a pond, demolition timber becomes an orangery. The last two are harder to point to, but they are just as real – and they are what this book is about.

Knowledge circulates when someone teaches what they know and someone else carries it on. The social cycle circulates when people give their time, their skill or their things – and get something back: a community, an experience, a dinner, a friend. On a place where these cycles work, something happens that is hard to measure but easy to feel: the place gains a soul that is larger than those who own it.
satt: Taster or in depth: ceramics, joinery, textiles, smithing, food, permaculture, forest gardening and reuse.
The year’s festivals and open days: Easter, Midsummer, the harvest festival, the Christmas market and open workshops.
A few days to create, to arrive or to think – with a tipi, sauna, natural pool and winter bathing.
Work days when we build, plant and harvest together – and eat afterwards.
principer: The place first.
Meetings should strengthen the place, not wear it out. We adjust numbers, times and activities to what the land, the animals and the neighbours can bear.
Doing together.
Almost everything we offer includes something you do with your hands – even a leadership programme.
The seasons decide.
We follow the rhythm of the garden. What can be done in May cannot be done in November, and vice versa.
Small groups.
Better twelve people who truly meet than a hundred who merely pass through.
Everyone contributes.
Whoever comes here brings something – a question, an experience, a plant – and leaves something behind.
rummen: Vreta Solglänta is 3,700 square metres, but it holds an unusually large number of rooms. Some have walls: the French country house, the Studio and the workshops – and the orangery. Others have only the sky for a roof: the long table under the oak, the meadow, the clearings of the forest garden, the pond and the fire. Each room has its character, and each meeting takes its shape from where it happens.

A conversation about leadership becomes a different one in a clearing than in a conference room. A ceramics course takes on another rhythm when there is a meadow to walk out into while the clay rests. A dinner becomes a feast when it is laid under the open sky on a light summer evening.
elden: Some of the place’s most important rooms are also the simplest. The outdoor fireplace, where groups gather on logs and blankets as it grows dark. The clearings in the forest garden, where a ring of chairs is enough for a conversation. And the stones – great blocks of granite that have lain on the place since the inland ice withdrew – which become natural places for stillness.
tipi_cards: Leadership groups, teams and associations gather around the fire – with no tables and no screens.
Meditations, ceremonies and storytelling in the evenings.
Rain shelter and gathering place for course days in the garden.
Music and food by the fire after Midsummer, harvest or the Christmas market.
tipi_p: In the meadow, at the edge of the forest garden, stands the tipi. It has a fire in the middle and the sky visible through the opening where the poles meet. It is perhaps the most elemental room on the place: a circle of people around a fire, with no table and no stage, where everyone can see one another.

The tipi is used for what needs a room of its own. Talking circles on leadership days. Evenings of storytelling and music. Meditations and ceremonies on the retreats. A rain shelter for course participants when the summer weather turns. And sometimes simply for sitting a while by the fire while the rest of the place sleeps.

The circle is no accident. When people sit in a ring there is no front row and no back row. Everyone is the same distance from the fire, and everyone can see one another’s faces. It changes the conversation. It becomes calmer, more attentive and more honest. Many groups who have sat in the tipi for an evening describe it as the moment they truly met.

The fire in the tipi demands respect. It is fed with dry wood from the place’s thinning, it is never left unattended and it is put out completely before the group leaves. During dry spells and fire bans we do not light it – then the tipi becomes a room for lanterns and candles instead.
kurser_tradgard: Forest gardening from the ground up
Plant layers, guilds and plant choices for a Nordic climate. We plan and plant a plant community around a fruit tree.
Ethics, the twelve principles, zones and sectors – applied to your own place.
Hot compost, bokashi, worm compost and leaf mould. How to read the health of the soil.
Leaning the soil, sowing and planting native species, cutting with a scythe and carrying away the hay.
Catching rainwater, building a pond with shallow edges and creating habitats.
Assessing, cleaning and building with reclaimed material – from raised beds to walls.
Observing and recording: photo points, species inventories and simple measurements.
Caring for fruit trees and propagating varieties suited to the climate.
kurser_verkstad: Two to four hours. A first meeting with a material – throwing, whittling, embroidery, smithing. You go home with something you have made yourself.
One or two days. Time to learn the basics properly and make a few more attempts. Lunch at the long table is included.
Four to eight sessions over a season. For those who want to become good at something – and follow a project from start to finish.

Keramik: The ceramics courses begin with the hardest part: centring the clay on the wheel. It takes time, and most people fail many times before it comes. But once it does, a new world opens. The tasters give a feel for the material. The weekend courses lead to your own bowls and cups. The course series follow the whole process – from clay to throwing, turning a foot ring, glazing and firing – and end with a shared firing day.
Snickeri och täljning: The whittling courses are the simplest way in: a knife, an axe and a fresh birch branch. In an afternoon it becomes a butter knife, in a weekend perhaps a spoon. In the joinery workshop you can then go on to furniture making, restoring old chairs and working with reclaimed timber – where both hand tools and machines are used, with a safety briefing for every machine.
Textil: In the sewing room there are courses in visible mending, embroidery and patchwork from exclusive fabric samples. The mending evenings are open: bring what you want to mend, and we help one another. The embroidery courses often take their motifs from the garden – a flower from the meadow, a leaf from the forest garden – and can be the start of something larger.
Smide, mat och dryck: The smithy, the dairy and the brewery are also open for courses: an introduction to smithing and knife making, making fresh cheese and cheese, and juicing days when the neighbours’ apples become juice. For those who want to start small there are simpler versions: butter and soured milk in the kitchen, juice at the press and shorter demonstrations in the smithy.
Måla och teckna: The artists’ studio offers courses in botanical drawing, watercolour and sketching in the field. The aim is not to become an artist in a weekend, but to learn to see. Whoever draws the same plant once a month for a year learns more about the garden than many textbooks can give.

Påsk – vårtecken och första sådd: Easter is the first festival of spring. The hens have started laying again, the first bulbs are showing and it is time to sow the first seeds indoors. We celebrate with a day of sowing and planting, when children and adults sow tomatoes, chillies and summer flowers in pots from the ceramics workshop. There is egg painting, Easter twigs (påskris) with feathers from our own hens and a simple lunch at the long table.
Midsommar – ängen i full blom: Midsummer (midsommar) is the brightest festival of the year, and it is celebrated in the meadow when it stands in full bloom. We pick flowers for crowns, raise the maypole, eat pickled herring, potatoes and strawberries at the long table and dance until it grows cool. Whoever wishes can pick seven kinds of flowers to lay under their pillow – and whoever wishes can take a dip in the natural pool when the night is at its lightest.
Skördefest och mustdag – hösten delas: When the apples ripen in September it is time for the harvest festival. Neighbours come with their own apples, the press is set out and the juice flows. The table is laid with what the forest garden has given: fruit, berries, nuts, roots and bread. The workshops are open, ceramics and textiles are shown, and the shop sells the season’s jam and juice.
Julmarknad – ljus i mörkret: In December we gather in the early darkness around lanterns and candles. The sauna is fired, and whoever dares takes a winter dip in the pond. The Christmas market is the workshops’ great day: ceramics, textiles, woodwork and ironwork are sold alongside jam, juice, honey and glögg (Swedish mulled wine). The fire burns, and in the orangery a simple Christmas dinner is laid among the citrus trees.

fester_ar: Easter: sowing, planting and the first festival of spring.
Open garden: planting, plant swap and courses.
Open workshop and late-summer evenings by candlelight.
Christmas market and light in the darkness.
retreat_teman: Presence and inner silence. What remains when everything inessential falls away?
Beginnings and possibilities. What wants to be born through me today?
Grounding and belonging. What do I need to anchor in my life?
Courage and change. What am I ready to leave behind?
Compassion and relationships. How can I meet the world with greater openness?
Intuition and the unconscious. What am I trying to see?
Creativity and expression. What do I want to give form to?
retreat_p: A retreat is different from a course. A course is about learning something. A retreat is about giving yourself time – to create, to rest, to think, to be with others or with yourself. It is about leaving the pace of everyday life behind, and letting the place, the rhythm and the community do part of the work.

At Vreta the retreats are small, usually eight to fourteen people, and they last from a weekend to five days. The days have a clear structure but plenty of air. Meals are eaten together. Mornings often begin in stillness. Evenings often end by the fire.
skapande: Painting retreat. Three days with an easel in the meadow, the pond in morning mist and the forest garden in evening light. We draw and paint, walk around without a sketchbook in order to see, and show one another what we have made on the last day. No demands for results.
Ceramics retreat. A few days in the ceramics workshop with time to throw, glaze and fire – and to let the clay take the time it needs.
ledarskap_p: Anyone who has worked with leadership and organisational development knows that the most important changes seldom happen in a conference room. They happen when people truly meet: when they see one another, trust one another and dare to say what needs to be said. That takes safety, presence and time. And it often takes surroundings different enough to break habits.

Vreta Solglänta is such a setting. There are no screens on the walls and no whiteboards waiting. There is a garden that shows how systems work, a fire to gather around, a long table to eat at and work to do together. For a leadership team, a team or a board, a day or two here can be a turning point.
ledarskap: Understand the system before you change it. Where is the energy, where is the friction?
Functions that support one another – in a garden and in an organisation.
Different perspectives give resilience. Uniform systems are fragile.
What grows slowly often grows strong. Plan for ten years, not for a quarter.
format: A day of conversation, shared work in the garden or the workshop and dinner at the long table.
Two days of strategy, relationships and reflection – in surroundings that break habits.
Three to five days for leaders who want to deepen their leadership and their presence.
Planning days for associations, boards and project groups.
ta_emot: A clear invitation with times, address, directions and what to bring
Someone to meet you at the gate and show you round
Signs that tell what you are seeing and where you may walk
Something to do straight away – a task, a cup of coffee, a question
A closing in which everyone gets to say something
platsen_forst: Better twelve who truly meet than a hundred who pass through.
Wild zones and shore edges are left in peace.
Sound, light and traffic are adjusted – and the neighbours are invited.
Fire, water and tools need supervision and clear rules.
arbetsdagar: A few times each season we invite people to work days. It might be planting a hedge, laying a stone wall, building a compost or picking apples. Everyone is welcome, whatever their knowledge. We work for a few hours, eat together and finish with a walk round to see what we have achieved. The work days are perhaps the clearest example of the social cycle: you give your time and get community, knowledge and a share of the place’s history back.
planera: What do you want to achieve? To learn something, celebrate something, arrive, think afresh or build relationships?
How many are you? We welcome day visits for groups of up to twenty people. For overnight stays there are twelve beds and the tipi.
When do you want to come? The season shapes what can be done – and how it feels.
For how long? An afternoon, a day, a weekend or several days.
What do you want to do with your hands? Almost every visit to Vreta includes something you do together.
planera_p: Anyone who wants to come to Vreta – for a course, an event, a retreat or a day with their group – can begin with a few simple questions. The answers help us shape a visit that suits both the group and the place.
efterord: This book closes a series about Vreta Solglänta. The first was about the place – the forest garden, the pond, the meadow and the cycles. The second about the workshops and the finds – the materials with a history and the hands that give them new life. This one is about the people – those who come here to learn, celebrate, create and think.

It is no accident that it comes last. People are what make everything else meaningful. A forest garden with nobody to harvest it is just a wood. A workshop with nobody making in it is just a room. A place without meetings is just an address.
Welcome to the table. Welcome to learn, to contribute and to come back.

forord: There is a particular kind of silence in a workshop. It is not the absence of sound – the wheel hums, the plane hisses, the hammer rings on the anvil, the loom thuds in its rhythm. It is something else. It is the concentration of someone learning something with their hands, who has for a while forgotten everything else.
This book is about that silence, and about the places where it arises.

In the first book about Vreta Solglänta we described the place as a living system: the forest garden, the meadow, the pond, the animals and the cycles that hold them together. The workshops were there too, but in the background. Here they take the leading role.
We have gathered seven workshops between two covers: the artists’ studio, the ceramics workshop, the joinery, the sewing and weaving room, the smithy, the dairy and the brewery.
principer: Materials with a history.
We begin with what already exists – given, collected, rescued or from the place itself. Every material and every tool should have a story we can tell.
No waste.
Offcuts and leftovers from one workshop become raw material in another – or go back to the soil.
Unique, not mass-produced.
We do not make the same thing in a hundred copies. Every object should have its own expression – and last a long time and be repairable.
Safe and lawful.
Fire, heat, tools and food demand respect. We follow the rules for fire safety, food hygiene and the making of alcohol.
Open to others.
The workshops are there to be shared. Whoever knows something teaches it; whoever wants to learn is welcome.
Old and new.
We use both hand tools and modern machines – whatever best serves the making.
fynd: Heartwood with tight growth rings, linseed-oiled and twenty years old. Won at auction – they become the load-bearing frame and timber framing of the orangery.
Hand-dressed slabs, two to four centimetres thick. Meant for the back wall of the orangery, an open fireplace and the wall behind the outdoor kitchen.
Seven bulk bags and a stack – an estimated two thousand or more old bricks from a dismantled chimney.

Sixteen plus four – twenty laminated panes, eleven millimetres thick, that were room dividers in a residence in Stockholm. Collected via Tiptapp (a Swedish collection app) – they wait for the orangery.
Trapezoidal sheeting from a demolished building – meant as the load-bearing layer under a sedum roof.
Window sections, small-paned frames and a batch of three-millimetre greenhouse glass – the basis of the orangery.
Late Neo-Renaissance from around 1900, with turned legs and original castors.
Exclusive upholstery samples, tapestries and curtain fabrics – raw material for patchwork, tablecloths and clothes.
fynd_p: To understand what that means in practice, it is enough to look back over a single year. This is a selection of what has found its way to Vreta – through adverts, gifts, auctions and collections.

The list could have been much longer – and it grows all the time. Roof tiles in quantity, awnings, white goods, mouldings and joinery. Neo-Renaissance cupboards with turned details and generations of paint. A whole salad bar from a Pizza Hut restaurant that closed, which can become a serving table at the long table or a chilled display cabinet in the shop. Granite blanks once meant for gravestones, pieces of marble and limestone. Insulated sandwich panels – stone wool between two metal sheets – that can become the walls of a store or a workshop. Iron and steel for the smithy. Old carts and iron-shod cartwheels, which carry flowers, become gates or stand as reminders of a time when everything was drawn by hand. Rhododendrons dug up from a garden that was being redone. Terrariums that can become growing capsules in the orangery. Old yellow brick that had lain unused for seventy years. A lorry that can become the place’s rolling store. And once a whetstone – an old sharpening tool of stone – that turned up in the soil at Vreta itself.
hamtning: It often begins with an advert. On Tiptapp someone is giving away their pots. On Blocket (the Swedish classifieds site) a batch of oak posts is for sale. On Facebook Marketplace someone wants to be rid of a whole chimney stack that has just been taken down. A glass sheet needs collecting in Södermalm, some railings in Knivsta, a door is to be dropped off on the way. Then the trailer is hitched up, and the round is planned like a small expedition: several stops, a list, time windows to keep and a car to come home fully loaded to Vreta in the evening.

It is a way of working, not an accident. Collecting what others let go of is the most concrete way to live with reuse. It takes time, planning, some muscle and a good ratchet strap. But it gives something no builders’ merchant can give: materials with character, at a fraction of the price, and meetings with people who are often glad that what they have cared for gets to live on.
