studion: The artists’ studio at Vreta is painting studio and studio in one. There are easels, worktables, room to dry canvases and paper, and above all light. A large north window gives the even, cool light painters have sought for centuries – light that changes little through the day and casts no hard shadows.

But the studio is more than a room. It is a way of looking. Botanical drawing, watercolour and sketching in the field have always been among the best ways to learn to see. Whoever draws a flower discovers how the leaves sit, how the petals fold, which insects visit it. It is no accident that many of the great naturalists – Linnaeus, the von Wright brothers, Darwin – either drew themselves or worked closely with those who did.

At Vreta, art is therefore not a decoration laid on top of the place. It is part of how we understand it. The sketches in the site journal, the plates in our books, the watercolours of the meadow in July – all of it is documentation, but it is also a form of attention. And attention is the foundation of all regenerative design.
keramik: The oldest ceramic objects we know of are more than 20,000 years old. It is no wonder people learned early to shape clay – it is found almost everywhere, it is mouldable when damp and it becomes hard and lasting when fired. Around Uppsala clay is part of the landscape; many gardens here rest on it.

The ceramics workshop at Vreta is a place for clay, glaze and kiln – and for art. There are electric wheels and an electric kiln, an old oak worktable, shelves of reclaimed timber and a stainless steel sink from a closed-down canteen kitchen. Much of the equipment has been given by or collected from potters and schools that have stopped or changed.

Practical vessels for the garden are made here. But above all, ceramics with an expression of their own are made here: sculptural vases, bowls with irregular forms and deep glazes, and tableware made for Vreta’s long table in particular – where no plate is exactly like another. It is not mass production, and it is not meant to be. Every object is an original.
bränning: There is a moment in the potter’s work that always feels like a small celebration: when the kiln is opened after a firing. Everything that has been shaped, dried and glazed over weeks or months is decided in a few hours of heat. Sometimes the result is better than you dared hope. Sometimes a glaze has run, a vessel cracked, a colour become something else entirely. The kiln always has the last word.

At Vreta we want to make the firing something people share. A firing day can gather everyone who has worked in the workshop over a period. Someone brings coffee and buns, someone has made their first vessel, someone has tried a new ash glaze from the wood stove. When the kiln has cooled and the door is opened, everyone stands there together.

Outdoors stands a wood-fired kiln – a simple construction of brick, partly reclaimed, where the firing becomes an event lasting a whole day and night. Wood firing gives surfaces no electric kiln can imitate: the ash flying through the kiln melts into a natural glaze, the flames leave traces of red and brown. It takes many hands, shifts at the fire and a great deal of wood from the place’s thinning. But that is exactly why it becomes a festival.
snickeri: The joinery is both the most practical and one of the most artistic of Vreta’s workshops. Raised beds, pergolas and details for the orangery are built here. But furniture and objects with an expression of their own are also made here: a chair whose seat is an old oak board with the nail holes still in it, a table whose legs were once a barn beam, a sculptural bowl turned from a fruit-tree trunk that blew down. None of it is made in series.

The timber comes from many places. Offcuts from building and renovation work, planks from demolished barns advertised on Blocket, oak and elm felled in someone’s garden, old doors and window frames from Tiptapp, and timber from the place’s own thinning. Here what would otherwise have been burned or taken to recycling is given a new life.

Reclaimed timber is often of better quality than new. Old timber from demolished barns and houses often comes from slow-grown trees with tight growth rings, and it has dried for decades. It is stable, strong and has a patina that cannot be imitated. But it also takes more work: nails have to be pulled, surfaces cleaned, and every piece assessed for rot, insect damage and old treatments.
sommeri: The sewing room – Vreta’s sewing studio – is the place for textiles, mending, embroidery and new life for cloth. There are sewing machines, a large cutting table and boxes full of fabrics waiting for their task. Much of the material is reused: old sheets, curtains, workwear and woollen garments that take on new forms.

Mending is perhaps the most important thing done here. Visible mending – where the repair is not hidden but on the contrary highlighted with contrasting thread and decorative stitches – has become a movement of its own. A mended knee patch is not a sign of poverty but of care. It tells that the garment matters.

Embroidery is the artistic side of the sewing room. With needle and thread you can draw – and the motifs are everywhere around. The meadow’s flowers, the forest garden’s berries, the birds by the pond. Embroideries that are art in their own right are made here: large textile works on coarse linen, embroidered portraits of plants, wall hangings that mix traditional stitches with a modern idiom. And tablecloths and napkins that belong with the ceramic tableware on the long table are made here.
vaveri: The weaving room is a room with a floor loom, a spinning wheel and space for dyeing yarn. Weaving is one of the most meditative crafts there is – the rhythm of treadles, shuttle and beater – and one of the most mathematical. Every pattern is a code of lifts and lowers, weaves and colour changes.

At Vreta we weave with materials whose origins we know: wool from sheep farms nearby, flax grown on a small scale on the place, and rags of worn-out textiles that become rag rugs – perhaps the most Swedish of all reuse crafts.
smedja: The smithy is a small building of stone and wood with a forge, an anvil and a wall full of tools. Smithing is one of the oldest and most fundamental crafts. For centuries every village had its smith, who made and mended everything from nails and hinges to ploughshares and horseshoes. Without the smith, farming came to a halt.

Today a smithy is a rarity, but interest in traditional smithing is growing. There is something special about shaping iron by hand: heating it until it glows, and then, with hammer and anvil, drawing it out, bending, upsetting and splitting it into a new form. It is powerful, precise and unexpectedly calm.
mejeri: Before the refrigerator, milk was a fresh product that had to be dealt with at once. The answer was preserving. The milk was left to sour into fil and filmjölk (Swedish soured milk). The cream was churned into butter, which was salted and kept for months. And the milk was made into cheese, which could be stored through the winter. On the summer farms (fäbodar) of the Nordic countries a whole culture grew up around this – with whey butter, whey cheese and goat’s cheese that made use of every drop, even the whey.

The dairy at Vreta is a small, clean room of tiles and wood, with a cheese vat, shelves for ageing and a cold room. Vreta has no dairy animals of its own, so the milk comes from a farm nearby. That is part of the point: the dairy becomes a link between Vreta and the farms that surround the place.
bryggeri: When the forest garden’s apple trees ripen they give more fruit than anyone can eat. It is one of the great joys of fruit trees – and one of the great problems. Apples that are not dealt with rot, attract wasps and become a burden instead of a gift.

The brewery is our answer. It is a small room with a fruit press, fermenting vessels, oak casks and bottles. Here the apples from Vreta – and from the neighbours’ gardens – can become juice, cider and vinegar. And with hops from the forest garden’s climbing layer and malt from local barley, it can also become beer.
mustdag: If there is one day of the year that sums up the idea behind the brewery, it is juicing day. One Saturday in September the press is set out. Neighbours come with bags, buckets and wheelbarrows full of apples from their own trees – apples that might otherwise have been left lying. Children sort out the rotten ones. Someone mills, someone presses, someone bottles.

Juicing day is the clearest example of how preserving can become community. Nobody can press a tonne of apples alone, but together it can be done in a day. Whoever brings apples takes juice home. The pressings go to the compost or the hens. And what is left over can be sold at the harvest festival or become cider and vinegar.

The juice keeps only a few days in the fridge if it is not treated. To make it keep longer it is pasteurised – heated to around 75–80 degrees and filled hot into clean bottles or bag-in-box. It is a simple but important step, and it calls for care with temperature and cleanliness.
lagning: There is a quiet change under way in how we see clothes. After decades of cheap fashion thrown away after a few wears, interest is growing in mending, altering and looking after what we already have. At Vreta we want to contribute to that change.

Visible mending is part of it. Instead of trying to hide a hole with stitches in the same colour, the mend is made into a decoration – embroidery in a contrasting colour, a patch of beautiful fabric, a darned pattern. The tradition exists in many cultures, from Japanese sashiko to the patched workwear of Swedish rural people. The garment gains a story, and whoever wears it gains a reason to keep it.

We hold sewing evenings where neighbours bring what they want to mend and learn from one another. Clothes swaps where what is no longer used finds a new owner. Courses in darning, patching and simple alterations. They are small things, but they change the relationship to clothes – and to the people and materials that made them.
taljning: Whoever wants to start with wood does not need a whole workshop. A whittling knife, a small axe and a fresh birch branch go a long way. Carving fresh wood – what in English is called green woodworking – is the oldest way of working wood, and it is surprisingly easy to get started.

Fresh wood is soft and yielding. It is split along the grain instead of sawn, which makes the parts stronger. A butter knife can be finished in an afternoon. A spoon takes longer – and most people who have carved their first spoon remember it for a long time.

The most important thing is to learn a few basic grips, so that the knife always moves away from the body or is under control. With a safe grip and a sharp knife, whittling is a safe craft even for children, under supervision. A blunt knife is more dangerous than a sharp one, because it slips.

berattelsen: Originals and small series with their own expression – never mass production.
Every object carries its story: material, origin and the person who made it.

efterord: There is a risk with a book like this. It can make craft sound romantic – something done in golden light with time to spare. It is not always like that. Craft is often heavy, dirty and frustrating. The clay cracks, the cheese goes wrong, the iron burns. It takes years to become good.

But that is exactly why it means something. Craft is one of the few areas where we still meet reality unfiltered. The material does not care how we feel or what we think it ought to do. It responds only to what we actually do. It is a form of honesty we need more of.

At Vreta we see the workshops as an extension of the same thought that carries the forest garden. Making use of what is there. Letting processes take the time they take. Building knowledge step by step and sharing it with others. Seeing every leftover as the start of something new.
Welcome in. Put on your apron. Begin with something small.

forord: Every place has a threshold. A spot where you leave the road and step into something else – where the gravel crunches differently, where the air smells of lilac or fresh-cut grass, where you slow down without quite knowing why. There stands the large corkscrew hazel we moved from Vallentuna, its twisted branches like a gateway of living wood. And there, just inside the lilac hedge, stands a farmhouse by the gate.

The house holds two things: a café and a shop. In the café there is coffee, tea and cordial, buns and bread from the wood-fired oven, a soup at lunchtime and cakes made with what the forest garden gives. In the shop there are plants and seeds, jam and honey, craft from the workshops, antiques and reclaimed finds, art from artists in the area, botanical plates from Vreta – and food and goods from producers within 150 kilometres.

It may sound a small thing, a café and a shop. But for a place like Vreta it is perhaps the most important building of all. It is the first thing you see and the last you leave. It is where the neighbour stops on the way home, where the cyclist refills a water bottle, where someone who has never heard of permaculture buys a plant and leaves with a question. It is where the economy of the place and its community meet.
troskeln: Along it stands the lilac hedge, a metre and a half high, and in the middle of it is the entrance. That is where everything begins: the post, the deliveries, the guests, the neighbours walking past with the dog. For a long time the entrance was just a gap in a hedge. Now it is something more – a place that says you are welcome before anyone has had time to say so.

The corkscrew hazel is already there. It is five metres high and three metres wide, with four or five stout stems and branches that twist like corkscrews. We moved it from Vallentuna in September and planted it at the entrance as a threshold tree: a living landmark at the passage from the road to the place. In time you can walk beneath its crown.

The farmhouse stands just inside, in the cart shed by the entrance, with the corkscrew hazel in front and the forest garden behind. From the road you see it through the trees: pale limestone, oiled oak, red windows and a roof of glazed tile and sedum. It does not look like a shop. It looks like a house that has always stood there – and happens to have its door open.
principer: The place first.
What is sold and served tells something about Vreta – about the soil, the craft or the reuse.
The season decides.
The menu and the shelves follow the year. What is not here right now has to wait.
The story comes along.
Every object and every jar has an origin the buyer is told about.
Near before far.
First what is made on the place, then within 150 kilometres, then the rest.
Nobody has to buy anything.
Whoever only wants to sit in the sun for a while is just as welcome as whoever shops.
system: Anyone who works with organisations as systems soon learns that it is seldom the individual parts that decide whether something works, but the relationships between them. A café that only sells coffee is a business. A café that sells coffee brewed in cups from the ceramics workshop, with buns baked in the outdoor kitchen from flour from a mill in the area and cordial from berries in the forest garden, is something else. It is a node in a network.

The café and the shop take in flows from the rest of the place – harvest, craft, finds, knowledge – and send others back: money, people, ideas and questions. The surplus from the forest garden becomes jam in the shop. The money from the jam becomes new berry bushes. A small shop can carry a whole place – if it is built as part of the place and not as an addition to it.
gardshus: When the orangery was drawn, we decided that the other buildings on the place would follow the same style. The farmhouse by the gate is one of them. It has the same family of materials: hand-dressed Syrian limestone in varying sizes, vertical boarding of reclaimed oak with an oiled finish, a plinth of rough stone in red-brown shades and large window sections with bright red frames, about 140 by 200 centimetres with nine panes. The roof has single-roll clay tiles with a red-brown glaze, of the same kind as the roughly 700 Monier tiles stored for the orangery – and partly sedum, which ties the house to the meadow and feeds the pollinators.

The facade lighting is galvanised and painted in the same warm grey-green as on the orangery. They are small details, but they are what make the houses at Vreta look as if they belong together – as if built by the same hands, with the same idea.
fika: There is no really good translation of fika. It is not just coffee, and it is not just a cake. It is the moment when you put down what you are doing, sit down and talk – or do not talk – with someone else. At workplaces fika is often when the most important conversations take place. In the garden it is the reward after a morning with the spade. Fika is a social institution disguised as a coffee break.

The café at Vreta is built around that idea. It is not a place where you buy a coffee to take away, but a place where you sit down. That is why there are no disposable cups. Coffee is served in cups from the ceramics workshop, and whoever wants to take their coffee along may borrow a jar – or buy a cup and take it home.

hellre: It is tempting to make a long menu. But every dish on a menu needs ingredients, time, fridge space and knowledge – and a small café with a few people behind the counter does best by doing a few things really well. So the menu at Vreta is short. Coffee and tea. Cordial and juice. Two or three kinds of bread and buns. A cake with whatever the forest garden gives right now. A soup or a salad at lunchtime. And a sandwich on sourdough bread.

Most of it is baked in the morning in the wood-fired oven in the outdoor kitchen or in the Cottage kitchen. What is not sold during the day becomes the next day’s bread pudding or croutons, and the rest goes to the compost. Nothing is thrown away needlessly.

shop_p: In the book about the workshops we described the shop as the workshops’ shop window – the place where what has been made meets its new owners. In the farmhouse it has a room of its own and a broader task. Here there are seven kinds of goods, all connected to the place in some way: plants and seeds from the forest garden, a larder of what is harvested, craft from the workshops, antiques and reclaimed finds, art from artists in the area, botanical plates from Vreta Regenerative Initiative and goods from producers within 150 kilometres.

What unites them is that they have an origin you can tell about. There are no shelves of a hundred identical mugs here. What is sold is unique objects, small series and the season’s produce – and when they are gone, they are gone.

antikt: An old object is often more than it seems. A cup may have a mark that reveals the factory and the year. A chair may be a copy or an original. A lamp may be attributed to a well-known designer, or merely resemble one. That is why every find is researched before it is sold – with a loupe, registers of marks, old catalogues, auction archives and sometimes a conversation with someone who knows more.

It is detective work, and one of the most enjoyable parts of all reuse. The knowledge that emerges is part of the value. Whoever buys a cup in the antiques corner is told what it is, where it comes from and roughly how old it is – and if we do not know for certain, we say so.
planscher: While working on the books about Vreta, a whole collection of pictures has grown: natural history plates in the spirit of the Finland-Swedish von Wright brothers, with birds, insects, plants and animals from the place; illustrations of the buildings and the garden; diagrams of the seven layers of the forest garden and the wheel of the year. They are made for the books, from our descriptions and sketches, but they also look good on a wall.

In the shop they are sold as plates and postcards: printed on thick, uncoated paper, rolled in paper and tied with linen twine, or framed in frames from the joinery. Some come in large format for anyone who wants a whole wall of meadow flowers. Others are small enough to send by post.
vonwright: Magnus, Wilhelm and Ferdinand von Wright grew up on the Haminanlax estate outside Kuopio in eastern Finland in the first half of the nineteenth century. They became known for their true-to-life paintings of birds, and Svenska foglar (Swedish Birds), which Magnus and Wilhelm published in 1828–1838, is counted among the great works of Swedish natural history illustration. Their pictures combine scientific precision with a warmth and liveliness that make you want to look for a long time.
That is the feeling we have tried to capture in Vreta’s plates – not as copies, but as a tribute to a way of seeing nature: closely, lovingly and with respect for every detail.
femtonmil: There is no legal definition of locally produced in Sweden. The word is used for everything from vegetables from the neighbour’s field to goods that have travelled across half the country. So we have set a limit for the shop and the café: 150 kilometres as the crow flies from Vreta Solglänta. Whatever is sold as local is made within that circle.

150 kilometres is not a random figure. It is roughly how far you can drive there and back in a day in an old lorry and still have time to talk to the person you are collecting from. It is near enough to visit the farm, the mill or the cheesemaker and see how it is done. And it is large enough to hold an unusual wealth of landscapes and produce.

From small-scale cheesemakers and farm dairies in Uppland and Västmanland.

cirkeln_p: Within 150 kilometres of the gate lie the plains of the Mälaren valley with grain and rapeseed, the coastal lands of Uppland and Roslagen with fishing and grazing, the forests and old ironworks towns of Västmanland and Dalarna, the farms and lakes of Södermanland – and across the sea Åland, with its orchards and sheep farming – although goods from there need a customs declaration, since Åland lies outside the EU’s tax area. Here there are mills and bakeries, cheesemakers and dairies, beekeepers, fruit growers, fishers, smokehouses, coffee roasters, breweries, wool spinners and potters. About a third of Sweden’s population lives within the same circle.

relationer: An ecosystem is not strong because it has many species, but because the species have many relationships.
oppet: The worst thing that can happen to a small café in the country is not that it is empty on a Tuesday. It is that someone has cycled twenty kilometres to get there and stands in front of a locked door. So the opening hours are few, clear and reliable. Better weekends and chosen days that always hold than weekdays that sometimes do.

The season decides. In May the café and the shop open at weekends, and in summer they are open several days a week. In autumn they are open at weekends and during events. In winter we stay closed, except for Advent and the Christmas market – and for courses and groups who book ahead.

forord: There is a particular kind of silence you can only experience by sleeping in a place. It comes in the evening, when the last guest has gone and the fire has died down, and it is still there in the morning before anyone else is awake. That is when you hear the garden: the blackbird in the apple tree, the wind in the reeds by the pond, the rain on the roof. Whoever only visits a place by day misses that silence. Whoever sleeps there gets it thrown in.

That is why you can sleep at Vreta Solglänta. Not as in a hotel, and not as in a hostel, but in a place where every room is a small world of its own and nature is always close. Six rooms with twelve beds: one in the Cottage, one in the artists’ studio, one in the orangery, two in the garden cabin and one above the joinery and the ceramics workshop.

The rooms are furnished like a concept hotel – each with its own expression – but in the same spirit as the rest of the place. Linen and wool bedding. Beautiful rugs on wide floorboards. Ceramics from the workshop, mirrors with a history, lamps that give a warm light. Some rooms are low and snug, others high and airy. Each is tied to a part of the place: the kitchen garden, the studio, the citrus trees, the orchard, the pond and the workshops.

The rooms are for many kinds of guest. For friends and family who want to stay the weekend. For participants in courses and retreats who need rest between the days. And for travellers who find their way here through a booking service and want to stay somewhere unlike anywhere else. The direction is clear: Vreta is a place where you do not only visit, but also stay.
vardskap: I have learned a great deal about leadership from receiving people. A good host does much the same things as a good leader: prepares in advance so that others need not think about the practical side, creates safety without controlling, and leaves room for the guest to find their own way of being in the place. It is the difference between being served and being welcomed.

For us it means that the rooms are ready when the guest arrives: made up with clean linen, a jug of water, a handwritten note, a sprig from the garden. It is easy to find, easy to understand and easy to feel at home. And then we can withdraw and let the place do the rest.
principer: Every room has a place.
The room takes its character from the part of Vreta where it lies.
Natural materials close to the body.
Linen, wool, cotton and wood in the bed – nothing that does not breathe.
Reuse with care.
Furniture, mirrors, rugs and lamps with a history, well cleaned and mended.
Light that warms.
Many small light sources with warm light – and darkness at night.
Easy to be a guest.
Everything you need is where you expect it to be.

Sängen först: Everything begins with the bed. It is where the guest spends most hours, and it decides whether a night is remembered as good or bad. That is why the beds are the one place where we do not compromise: good mattresses, generous duvets and pillows – and bedding in natural materials. Linen that grows softer with every wash. Cotton in sateen or percale. Wool blankets at the foot for the cold nights, and a sheepskin to put your feet on when you get up.

Linen is one of the oldest textile materials in the Nordic countries. It breathes, it does not overheat in summer, and it grows more beautiful the older it gets. Some of the linen at Vreta comes from house clearances and auctions – hand-woven sheets with monograms, embroidered pillowcases, thick towels of half-linen. The rest comes from the sewing room, where new linen is sewn into duvet covers and curtains.
Mattor och golv: The floors at Vreta are wooden – wide planks worn by generations of feet. The rugs make them warm. Long-pile rya rugs, kilims in deep colours, rag rugs woven from old clothes. A rug by the bed is the first thing you feel in the morning, and it should feel good.
Keramik i varje rum: There are ceramics from the workshop in every room. Lamp bases in a moss-green glaze, a jug and a glass for water, a bowl for jewellery and keys, a vase with a sprig from the garden. In the washrooms stand handmade stoneware basins on slabs of Carrara marble – the marble comes from a kitchen worktop given away via Tiptapp.
Speglar: A mirror changes a room. It catches the light from the window and spreads it; it makes a small room larger and a dark room lighter. Old mirrors also have something new ones lack: a faint silvery shimmer, a carved or gilded frame, a sense of having reflected many faces before yours. We find them at auctions, in house clearances and at flea markets – and they hang in almost every room.
Ljuset: The light sets the mood more than anything else. No harsh ceiling lights, but many small light sources at a low height. Many were bought at auction: a pair of wall lamps attributed to Carl Fagerlund and probably from Orrefors, bronze wall sconces, brass lamps from EWÅ in Värnamo, wall lamps with fabric shades and a collection of seven window lamps. They now sit by beds and in windows in the rooms: a reading lamp by the bed, a ceramic lamp on the chest of drawers, candles in lanterns. Warm light in the evening, and true darkness at night – with blackout curtains for those who want them and thin linen curtains for those who want to wake with the sun.

natten: When it gets dark at Vreta, it gets truly dark. There are few street lamps and almost no light from neighbours, and on a clear night the Milky Way shows. It is one of the place’s greatest assets, and we protect it: the outdoor lighting is low, warm and directed downwards, and it is switched off when it is not needed.

In the dark another world wakes. The bats hunt over the pond, the tawny owl calls at the edge of the woods, the hedgehog hunts slugs in the beds and the moths seek out the honeysuckle. Whoever steps out for a while with a lantern before bed sees some of it.
morgonen: Morning at Vreta begins with the birds. The blackbird is first, often before it is light, followed by the robin, the chaffinch and the willow warbler. Whoever sleeps with the window open, or in the tipi, wakes to a choir no alarm clock can match.
frukost: Breakfast at Vreta is served in the Cottage kitchen or in the orangery – or on a tray in bed for those who want it. Bread from the wood-fired oven, eggs from the hens, jam and berries from the forest garden, cheese and coffee in ceramic cups. It is one of the things guests remember longest.
tipi: There is something ancient about sleeping in a ring. Nobody lies first or last, everyone sees one another, and the fire in the middle keeps both the warmth and the conversation alive. Many who have slept in the tipi describe it as the best night of their whole stay – not because it is the most comfortable, but because it is the closest.

The fire demands respect. Whoever sleeps in the tipi is given a briefing on fire and safety, the fire is kept small at night, and there is always an extinguisher and a fire blanket at the entrance. During dry spells and fire bans we sleep in the tipi without a fire – with more blankets and lanterns instead.
tipi_cards: Mattress, sheepskin, wool blanket and linen pillow.

ateljen: The artists’ studio is built for the light. Tall north windows give an even, still light that changes little over the day – the light painters have sought for centuries. At night it becomes a bedroom, and whoever sleeps here wakes to the same light the paintings have grown in.

The bed stands free in the room, with white linen and an ochre wool blanket. A large gilded mirror leans against the wall and catches the windows. Paintings lean along the walls, an easel waits in the corner, and on the floor lies a kilim on wide planks. The simple studio kitchen – from a house in Djursholm – is in the same building, with coffee and tea.
citron: The orangery is ten metres long, five metres wide and five metres high, built of oak posts, reused windows and a back wall of Syrian limestone. Up in the loft, under the glass roof, there is room for a double bed. From here you look down over the citrus trees, the figs and the kitchen – and up at the sky. At night the stars show through the glass, and in the morning the sun arrives before anyone else.

The loft is separated from the rest of the orangery by laminated glass – some of the twenty panes that were once room dividers in a residence in Stockholm. Laminated and sound-dampening, they let the light through but keep out the noise from the kitchen below. It is one of the best examples of how a find can land in exactly the right place.
regler: Letting rooms brings responsibility. Every room has a smoke alarm and an extinguisher, and escape routes are clearly marked. Candles always stand in lanterns and are put out before you fall asleep. Letting follows the rules that apply to short-term rentals, with insurance covering guests and damage. There are clear rules on pets and smoking, and quiet hours are respected – for the guests’ sake and the neighbours’.
efterord: There is a difference between visiting a place and staying in it. Whoever visits sees the place as it is by day – with work, conversation and activity. Whoever stays sees it when nobody is showing it off: in the dark, at dawn, in the rain. That is when you understand what a place really is.

The rooms at Vreta are made of what others have let go of – sheets from house clearances, mirrors from auctions, decking from a balcony, glass from a residence, oak from a demolished building. But what makes them rooms to remember is what happens in them: conversations that go on after the light is out, mornings with coffee on the steps, nights with rain on the roof.
lagt: Sheets, pillowcases and curtains. Breathes and grows more beautiful with the years.
Blankets and sheepskins. Warms, regulates moisture and cleans itself.
Rya, kilim and rag rug on wide wooden floors.

forord: If you want to understand a place, go to the kitchen. It is where people gather when the party is really over, where the children sit on the bench licking spoons, where someone stands stirring a pot while someone else lays the table and a third tells something that makes everyone laugh. The kitchen is the heart of the place – not because the food is cooked there, but because life is.

At Vreta Solglänta there are four kitchens, and several places where the fire is the kitchen. The Cottage kitchen, renovated last autumn and already the living room of the place. The orangery kitchen: sixty square metres under a five-metre ceiling, with a reclaimed kitchen from a flat on Hornsgatan in Stockholm, chandeliers made of cartwheels and lamps that look like artichokes. The outdoor kitchen, with Syrian limestone, ceiling panels from Algeria, grills, a wood-fired ceramic oven and Neo-Renaissance cupboards that have become a bar. And the studio kitchen in the artists’ studio – the simplest, from a house in Djursholm, where the coffee is brewed and lunch is eaten with paint on your hands.

And then the fire. The grill places where the muurikka griddle sizzles for thirty people, where a whole lamb or a whole pig is turned over the embers for a whole afternoon, where big pots simmer and cast-iron pots lie buried in the embers with coals on the lid.
ateranvand: None of the kitchens was bought new in a shop. The Cottage kitchen has grown out of what was there and what was found: stone slabs, a granite shelf, brass candlesticks and copper. The orangery kitchen comes from a flat on Hornsgatan in Stockholm, where it was taken out when someone else wanted something new. The ceiling panels in the outdoor kitchen come from Algeria. The cupboards in the bar are Neo-Renaissance and have had at least one life before Vreta. The studio kitchen comes from a house in Djursholm – the one we collected in spring, not the one from the autumn.

It is the same thought that shapes the rest of the place: most of what we need already exists. A kitchen from the 1990s or the 1950s can be of far better quality than a new one from a department store – solid wood, real fittings, stone worktops that last for generations. It takes adaptation and sometimes a little imagination. But the result is kitchens with character that nobody else has.
elden: Out on the plot are the grill places – hearths built of stone for cooking for many. They are Vreta’s fifth kitchen, and in a way the most elemental. Here food is cooked the way people have done it for thousands of years: over an open fire, in large vessels, slowly and together.

Cooking over fire takes time and attention. The fire has to be lit in good time and allowed to burn down to embers. The heat has to be read and adjusted. The food has to be turned, stirred and watched. But that is exactly why it becomes a community. Someone tends the fire, someone chops vegetables, someone turns the spit – and everyone stands round the fire talking.
eld_respekt: Cooking over an open fire demands respect. The hearths are built of stone and have plenty of clear space around them. We always have water and a fire blanket close by, and the fire is never left unattended. During dry spells and fire bans we cook on gas in the outdoor kitchen instead. And we use dry wood from the place’s thinning – never treated timber.
regler: When we serve food to groups and to the public we follow food law. That means good hygiene, a cold chain, allergen labelling and registration with the municipality. It applies to the food over the fire too – perhaps especially there.
